name: Message Ordering and Partitioning
intent: Keep the order that matters (per account, per order) while still scaling out consumers, by partitioning messages on a key instead of promising a global order.
scenario: Account events (deposit, withdraw) for many accounts flow through one topic. A withdrawal must never be processed before the deposit that funds it, but the topic must also scale past one consumer, and a few busy accounts send most of the traffic.
problem: A single queue with a single consumer is perfectly ordered but is capped at what one consumer can process. Adding competing consumers scales throughput but a later message can finish first, and a retried message arrives after its successors, so a withdrawal can run before its deposit. Total order across everything cannot be scaled; the real question is which order is actually needed, and how to keep exactly that.

howItWorks.title: Competing consumers trade order for throughput
howItWorks.text: N workers pull from one queue and each message goes to one of them. Two messages for the same account can be in flight at once on different workers with different processing times, so the later one can finish first. A failed message that is redelivered after a visibility timeout (how long a taken message stays hidden) also lands behind messages that were sent after it. Standard SQS and RabbitMQ with several consumers behave like this; the ordering you get is 'roughly FIFO'.

howItWorks.title: Partition by the entity that must stay ordered
howItWorks.text: A partitioned log (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar) splits a topic into partitions. The producer picks the partition from the message key, typically hash(key) mod partitionCount (Kafka's default partitioner uses murmur2). Each partition is an append-only log with increasing offsets (position numbers), so order holds inside a partition and nowhere across partitions. Pick the key as the unit of ordering: the account id or order id, not a random id and not the event type.

howItWorks.title: A consumer group owns whole partitions
howItWorks.text: In a consumer group (consumers that share the work of a topic) each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, which reads it in offset order. That is the guarantee that keeps per-key order. It also means useful parallelism is at most the partition count: with 8 partitions the ninth consumer is idle. Several partitions can share one consumer, but one partition is never split across consumers.

howItWorks.title: Hot keys make hot partitions
howItWorks.text: Partitioning balances keys, not load. If one account sends 30% of the events, its partition and its consumer carry at least 30% of the work no matter how many other partitions or consumers exist, so the slowest partition sets the throughput of the whole topic. Options are salting a key (which gives up order for that key), a dedicated topic for known hot keys, or making the handler faster.

howItWorks.title: Retries and resizing are where order silently breaks
howItWorks.text: A failed message sent to a retry topic or put back at the tail is applied after its successors. To keep order you either retry in place (the partition is blocked, so one poison message stalls its whole partition) or make the consumer order-tolerant. Changing the partition count changes hash(key) mod n, so a key moves to another partition while its old events may still be queued on the previous one, and a new event can overtake them.

howItWorks.title: Make consumers tolerate disorder
howItWorks.text: Give each entity a per-key sequence number or version. The consumer stores the last applied version and ignores anything not newer (version-aware, idempotent), or holds back an event that skips ahead until the gap is filled (gap detection, a reorder buffer). This is the same idea as the sequence numbers behind causal order: you only need order between events that are related, not between everything.

pros: Per-key order is preserved while consumers run in parallel across keys
Throughput scales with partitions and consumers, with no coordination on the hot path
A partition is a simple, replayable log, so a consumer can re-read from an offset
Order-tolerant consumers make retries, redelivery and replays safe
cons: No order across partitions: 'all events in the system' is not available at scale
Parallelism is capped by the partition count, and adding partitions later breaks key placement
Hot keys create hot partitions, and the slowest partition limits the whole topic
Strict order and retries conflict: blocking a partition for one bad message costs latency for every key on it
whenToUse: Events about an entity (account, order, device) that must be applied in order, such as ledgers, state machines and change feeds
High-volume topics that must scale past one consumer
Pipelines that rebuild state from a log and need the same result on every replay
whenNotToUse: Independent tasks (emails, thumbnails) where order does not matter: plain competing consumers are simpler and balance load better
When you truly need one global total order at high rate: a single partition or a sequencer is a throughput ceiling, so reconsider the requirement first
When a very small number of keys carries most of the traffic and each must be both ordered and fast: partitioning cannot help
pitfalls: Keying by something other than the entity, such as a random message id or the event type, silently gives no useful order
Adding partitions to a live topic: hash(key) mod n changes, so keys move while old events are still queued and order breaks during the transition (and compacted topics see one key in two places)
Retry topics and dead-letter queues that re-publish a failed message behind its successors, reordering the key
Calling async handlers inside a consumer without awaiting them, or processing a batch on a thread pool, which throws away the order the partition gave you
Over-provisioning partitions: the guarantee does not need thousands, and each partition costs file handles, replication and rebalance time
Assuming the producer preserves order: with several in-flight requests and retries the client can reorder unless idempotent or ordered sending is enabled

roles.label: Producer
roles.description: Sends events and chooses the partition, usually from the message key.

roles.label: Partition
roles.description: An append-only log. Order holds inside one partition and nowhere across partitions.

roles.label: Consumer
roles.description: A member of a consumer group that owns whole partitions and applies their events.

quiz.question: A Kafka topic has 12 partitions and a consumer group of 12. The producer sets each message key to a random UUID. Sometimes a withdrawal for an account is processed before the deposit that funds it. What is the right fix?
options: Key by account id so one account's events share a partition
Double the partition count to 24 so events spread more evenly
Use the event type as the key so deposits are always handled first
Add more consumers so each message is processed faster
quiz.explanation: Order exists only inside a partition, and a random key scatters one account's events across all of them. Keying by the entity that must stay ordered puts them in one partition read in offset order. More partitions or consumers do not create order, and keying by event type would put all deposits together instead of keeping one account's events together.

quiz.question: A topic has 6 partitions and one consumer group with 6 instances. Lag (the number of messages waiting) is growing, so the team scales the group to 12 instances. Lag does not improve. Why?
options: The group is still rebalancing, and lag will drop once the new assignment settles
Each partition goes to one consumer in the group, so six instances sit idle
Consumers in a group share a partition, which adds coordination overhead
Per-key order forces all instances to take turns on one shared offset
quiz.explanation: A partition is never split across consumers in a group, so useful parallelism is capped at the partition count. To go faster the topic needs more partitions or a faster handler. A rebalance would settle within seconds, not leave lag flat.

quiz.question: A consumer processes events for account 7 in order. When 'withdraw 50' fails with a database timeout, it publishes the event to a separate retry topic and carries on with the next message. A later 'withdraw 80' for the same account succeeds. What is the risk?
options: The partition stays blocked until the retry succeeds, delaying every other account on it
The retry topic drops the event, because a message can be consumed once per group
The consumer group rebalances and every account replays from the start
The retried event is applied after later events, breaking that account's order
quiz.explanation: Moving a failed message to another topic puts it behind its successors, so it is applied late. Blocking the partition is what retry in place does, which keeps order but stalls other keys. Per-key version numbers in the consumer make late events safe.
